title: How two cameras find a drone
summary: Test fixture, hand-written (not from OpenRouter). Two scenes on triangulation, used by the test suite and the dry-run demo.

scenes.title: One camera is not enough
scenes.learning_goal: A single camera gives a direction, not a distance.
scenes.visual_plan: A camera icon on the left, a drone dot on the right, a ray from the camera through the drone that keeps going.

lines.speaker: learner
lines.text: If a camera sees a drone, doesn't it know where the drone is?
lines.visual: A camera shape appears at left. A small drone dot appears at upper right.

lines.speaker: host
lines.text: It knows the direction. Every point on this ray looks the same to that camera.
lines.visual: A ray draws from the camera through the drone and on to the frame edge. Two ghost drone dots appear on the ray, nearer and farther.

lines.speaker: learner
lines.text: So the drone could be close and small, or far away and big.
lines.visual: The near ghost dot shrinks and the far ghost dot grows, then both fade out.

scenes.title: Two rays meet at one point
scenes.learning_goal: Two cameras give two rays; where they cross is the drone.
scenes.visual_plan: Add a second camera at the bottom right. Draw its ray. Highlight the crossing point and label it.

lines.speaker: host
lines.text: Now add a second camera somewhere else. It draws its own ray toward the drone.
lines.visual: A second camera appears at lower right. A second ray draws toward the drone in amber.

lines.speaker: learner
lines.text: And the drone has to be where the two rays cross.
lines.visual: The crossing point pulses. A green ring appears around it with the label 'drone'.

lines.speaker: host
lines.text: Exactly. That crossing is called triangulation.
lines.visual: The word 'triangulation' appears under the diagram, and the triangle between both cameras and the drone fills lightly.
